content: Barbital, also known as barbitone and marketed under the brand name Veronal, was the first barbiturate to be commercially available. It was widely used as a hypnotic agent to treat insomnia from 1903 until the mid-1950s. Chemically, barbital is referred to as diethylmalonyl urea or diethylbarbituric acid, with the molecular formula (C2H5)2C~CO NH]ICO. A sodium salt form of barbital, known as sodium 5,5-diethyl barbiturate, was also developed. The synthesis of barbital was first achieved in 1902 by German chemists Emil Fischer and Joseph von Mering. Their findings were published in 1903, and the compound was subsequently marketed in 1904 by Bayer under the trade name Veronal. The preparation of barbital involved condensing diethylmalonic ester with urea in the presence of sodium ethylate or reacting ethyl iodide with the silver salt of malonylurea. The resulting product was a white crystalline powder that was odorless and had a slightly bitter taste. A soluble form of barbital, marketed as Medinal, was introduced by the Schering company. Barbital was primarily prescribed for insomnia caused by nervous excitability and was available in capsule or cachet form. The recommended therapeutic dose ranged from 10 to 15 grains (approximately 0.65 to 0.97 grams). However, doses of 3.5 to 4.4 grams were considered lethal. Despite this, there were cases where individuals survived prolonged sleep lasting up to ten days after taking the drug. Veronal was regarded as a significant advancement over earlier hypnotics. Its slightly bitter taste was considered more tolerable compared to the strong, unpleasant taste of bromides, which were commonly used at the time. Additionally, it had relatively few side effects, and its therapeutic dose was well below the toxic threshold. However, prolonged use of barbital led to the development of tolerance, necessitating higher doses to achieve the desired hypnotic effect. This tolerance, combined with its slow-acting nature, contributed to cases of fatal overdoses, which were not uncommon.
